meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It ain't over till it's over'?
meta.ogDescription: Yogi Berra owns the sentiment. The famous wording isn't in the 1973 record — what the New York Post printed that September was rougher.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1925–2015 · Yankees catcher, Mets manager, accidental aphorist
answer.sourceLine: Berra is credited with this line everywhere, and he printed it under his own name in The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said! (Workman, 1998), dating it to the New York Mets’ 1973 pennant race — but no 1973 source has been found containing that wording. Etymologist Barry Popik, whose dated chronology is the standard reference here, writes plainly that “This exact quote hasn’t been found”; what the New York Post actually printed on 4 September 1973 was Berra saying “Yeah, it’s running out, but you’re still not out of it until it’s automatic.”

source.heading: What the 1973 record actually holds

docMeta.dd: New York Mets’ 1973 National League East pennant race

source.excerpt: Yeah, it’s running out, but you’re still not out of it until it’s automatic.
trail: 1892 — the sentiment is already a baseball adage with no owner: the Lawrence (KS) Daily Journal, 11 April 1892, p. 2, has “a game is never out till it is played out.” Popik notes no particular person has been credited with it. The Big Apple ↗

4 September 1973 — what Berra is actually on record saying during the Mets’ run, in the New York Post, p. 64, col. 1: “Yeah, it’s running out, but you’re still not out of it until it’s automatic.” Popik on ADS-L ↗

1975, then 1984 — the wording tightens in print while his name stays attached. Cincinnati Enquirer, 15 June 1975, p. 1-C: “in the immortal words of Yogi Berra, ‘The game’s not over ’til it’s over.’” Sports Illustrated, 2 April 1984: he knows a managing job, like a ball game, “ain’t over ’til it’s over.” The Big Apple ↗

1998 — Berra prints the polished line himself, in The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said! (Workman Publishing), tied to the 1973 Mets. It is the source Wikiquote gives, and the only one anybody gives. Internet Archive ↗
source.excerptNote: Berra’s answer when asked whether time was running out on the Mets, transcribed by Barry Popik from the New York Post of 4 September 1973, p. 64, col. 1 — the same citation he first posted to the American Dialect Society list in 1999. ADS-L, 10 October 1999 ↗ Pitcher List reports that the headline it answered read “Time is Running Out on the Mets.” Pitcher List ↗ This is the closest thing to the famous line in the 1973 record — and it is not the famous line.

source.rightsNote: Nothing in this trail is public domain in the United States. The only work that carries the exact wording under Berra’s name is The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said! (Workman Publishing, 1998), and every newspaper citation in the chronology — 1973, 1975, 1979, 1984 — falls well after the 1931 US public-domain threshold. Where the exact sentence was first coined remains undocumented, so treat the wording as in copyright rather than free to reuse.

author.name: Yogi Berra
author.heading: Who he was
author.metaLine: 1925–2015 · Yankees catcher, three-time AL MVP, Mets manager
author.bio: Lawrence Peter “Yogi” Berra caught for the New York Yankees from 1946 to 1963, won ten World Series titles as a player — more than anyone in major-league history — took three American League MVP awards (1951, 1954, 1955), made 18 All-Star teams, and entered the Hall of Fame in 1972. He then managed: the Yankees in 1964, the Mets from 1972 to 1975, and the Yankees again in 1984–85. He became at least as famous for his looping, self-cancelling one-liners, and was unusually honest about how slippery the record was — he titled his own 1998 collection I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said!

misattribution.heading: Right man, tidied-up words
misattribution.intro: Nobody argues this belongs to someone else. The problem is narrower and more common than a misattribution: the sentence everyone quotes is smoother than anything anyone recorded Berra saying at the time.

items.why: Barry Popik’s chronology puts it plainly: “This exact quote hasn’t been found, but Berra did say in September 1973…” — and what follows is the New York Post of 4 September 1973, p. 64, col. 1: “Yeah, it’s running out, but you’re still not out of it until it’s automatic.” The Big Apple ↗

items.scope: The phrasing was in the air
items.who: Red Holzman, New York Knicks coach
items.why: Popik logs the Asbury Park (NJ) Evening Press of 20 October 1973, p. 11: “The Knicks learned that, as coach Red Holzman phrased it, ‘that a ball game isn’t over until it’s over.’” That is not a claim Holzman coined anything — it is evidence that the construction was circulating in 1973 sports pages beyond Berra. The Big Apple ↗

Pitcher List’s fact-check names a New York Times piece of 30 May 1982 by the future senator Joe Lieberman — “As Yogi Berra said, ‘it ain’t over till it’s over’” — as the first appearance of the precise phrase it could locate, and notes this is still someone quoting Berra rather than a record of him speaking. Pitcher List ↗

Berra printed the line in The Yogi Book: I Really Didn’t Say Everything I Said! (Workman Publishing, 1998) and tied it to his 1973 Mets. Internet Archive ↗ Wikiquote accordingly files the line in its sourced “Yogiisms” section, sourced to that book and nothing earlier. Wikiquote ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The safest true sentence: the thought is Berra’s and he claimed the line in print himself, but the famous wording is not documented from 1973 — the contemporaneous record is a rougher sentence in the New York Post of 4 September 1973, and the sentiment itself was a baseball adage by 1892. The Big Apple ↗

context.heading: The comeback that made the line worth saying
lead: Berra took over the Mets in 1972 and by midsummer 1973 was managing a last-place team. Wikipedia’s account of the season has the Mets trailing the Chicago Cubs by 9½ games in the National League East in July; they went on to win the division and reach the World Series. Wikipedia ↗ That is the summer the line is always dated to, and it is why it stuck: the manager who said the season wasn’t finished turned out to be right.

What survives from that September, though, is rougher than the version on the poster. Popik’s chronology records the New York Post of 4 September 1973, p. 64, with Berra answering a question about time running out: “Yeah, it’s running out, but you’re still not out of it until it’s automatic.” Same thought, none of the polish. The Big Apple ↗
context.detailsSummary: The sentiment is older than Berra
detailsBody: The underlying adage predates him by generations. Popik’s earliest citation is the Lawrence (KS) Daily Journal of 11 April 1892, p. 2: “a game is never out till it is played out.” He notes that no particular person has been credited with the adage. The Big Apple ↗

The tightening happens across the following decade of newsprint, and Berra’s name rides along with it. Popik logs the Cincinnati Enquirer of 15 June 1975, p. 1-C — “Or, in the immortal words of Yogi Berra, ‘The game’s not over ’til it’s over’” — the New York Times of 23 August 1979, p. B11 with “It’s never over until it’s over,” and Sports Illustrated of 2 April 1984, which has Berra knowing that a managing job, like a ball game, “ain’t over ’til it’s over.” The Big Apple ↗
